idiom_name: copy-then-publish: build the replacement, commit with one assignment or atomic.Pointer[T].Store
implementation_notes: Go has no constructors, destructors or operator overloading, so the pattern reduces to its ordering: construct the replacement completely (deep-copying whatever the value points at -- maps, slices, pointers), then publish it with a single assignment or, for state read by other goroutines, atomic.Pointer[T].Store of a pointer to an immutable snapshot; the garbage collector reclaims the previous snapshot once the last loader releases it. Value types give the copy half for free (dst := *src) but only shallowly, and the commit -- one assignment or one atomic store -- cannot fail, which is exactly what the C++ idiom buys with a noexcept swap. The classic structure is neither available nor needed; what replaces its swap is the rule that a published snapshot is never mutated. Where the struct owns an unshareable resource (an *os.File, a sync.Mutex, an io.Closer), that field must not change owners during the commit: keep it behind a pointer owned by one goroutine, or guard in-place updates with sync.RWMutex instead.
pitfalls: A published snapshot must be immutable: mutating a map reached through Load races with readers and go test -race reports it -- always build a fresh map or slice, never edit the old one and Store it back.
atomic.Pointer[T] must not be copied after first use (go vet flags a struct that embeds it by value), and concurrent writers doing Load-build-Store lose updates unless CompareAndSwap retries.
Snapshot reuse breaks the guarantee: returning a value to a sync.Pool right after Store hands the memory to a new writer while readers still hold it; leave reclamation to the GC or reference-count.

GC replaces the destructor, so nothing releases the old state deterministically: handles, buffers or C memory that must be freed need an explicit close path that does not run while an old snapshot is reachable.
